title: Present the final soil report and improve a missing skill
intro: Complete a one-page report from your own supervised Plot C work. State what your pH and texture evidence supports, suggest two conditional crop candidates and at least one management next step. A report, self-rating or second attempt cannot substitute for observed practical competence.
goals: Submit a one-page Plot C report identifying the sample, date, purpose, real pH and texture method/results, interpretation, two conditional crop candidates and at least one supported management action with limitations.

Compare personal data with the separate pH 6.8/loam and pH 5.8/sandy-loam models, state what pH and texture alone cannot prove, and trace every final-review task to its own answer or performance evidence.
Use specific feedback to practise the affected skill and submit a new performance record; allow another 'not yet demonstrated' decision if a criterion is still missing.
Read the course result as a combination of online knowledge evidence and individually observed practical evidence, with each unobserved skill left visibly unassessed.

reading.title: 1. Put each result behind its evidence
paragraphs: A soil technician acts like an investigator: identify the sampling area, collect the sample under supervision, use the actual approved pH and texture procedures, inspect what each result says and report a reasoned recommendation. The grower's season depends on more than two tests; pH and mineral texture do not by themselves reveal all fertility, salinity, drainage, climate or crop constraints.

The final task checks safe precise procedure, interpretation, communication and willingness to practise a missing skill. A polished report is evidence for reporting and reasoning; each physical technique needs a separate individual trainer record. Do not turn a group result, a remembered model or a self-rating into a measured skill.

Act as a junior agricultural technician advising a local grower about Plot C and a coming crop season. Preserve the five report sections within one page. The source's 20-minute writing period is active writing after staged practical work; genuine drying and pH equilibration are separate. Do not substitute the bank's Field B or Paddock 3 records for Plot C.

reading.title: 2. Write one page from your Plot C record
paragraphs: Keep five clear sections within the one-page Plot C report: (1) title/identity heading with learner name, actual date and field/location; (2) introduction stating the test purpose; (3) results identifying the sample, methods, actual raw pH and texture evidence; (4) interpretation and discussion of what those results support and their limits; (5) recommendations with two conditional crop candidates and at least one justified management action. The title is a heading on that page, not an extra cover sheet. The source's approximately 20-minute active writing block follows the staged practical work; actual drying, instrument preparation and pH equilibration take their own recorded time. Mark unavailable data honestly in a pending draft, without copying a model value or claiming the completed actual-results report.

Use Plot C consistently for this ongoing task and its report. Explain the texture from observed ribbon/feel or documented percentage method. Put limitations beside crop and amendment choices, including climate, water, drainage, salinity and lab nutrient data not measured here.

reading.title: 3. Learn from the pH 6.8 and loam model
paragraphs: The supplied Plot C teaching model has pH 6.8 and loam texture. It suggests tomatoes and corn, annual compost and pH monitoring every 1–2 years. Keep those exact figures, crops and intervals as the source example, never as the learner's observation or a mandatory management schedule. Tomatoes and corn also depend on climate, water, season, salinity, nutrients and actual field structure.

A loam label often signals a useful particle-size balance, and pH 6.8 is neutral under the cited USDA-NRCS and Oregon State University Extension reaction classes. These facts do not prove that the entire soil is in 'excellent condition'. Check a site- and crop-specific lab report and field observations before asserting health or prescribing compost quality, rate or frequency. Here 'neutral' names a soil-reaction class; 6.8 remains below 7 and chemically near neutral. State the classification used.

reading.title: 4. Compare a different pH 5.8 sandy-loam example
paragraphs: Another source example uses pH 5.8 and sandy loam, with a 0.5-inch ribbon and gritty feel. USDA-NRCS and Oregon State University Extension classify pH 5.8 as moderately acidic; the source's 'slightly acidic' label is inconsistent with those cited scales. Low pH may affect nutrient availability, while sandy loam can have relatively rapid drainage and lower retention under some structures. Those are questions to check, not a complete diagnosis.

Potatoes and strawberries are the example crop pair, with corn also mentioned if further conditions fit. Retain them as candidates, not a guaranteed field plan. In the separate illustrative move from pH 5.8 toward 6.5, the source names corn and alfalfa as examples of broader crop options and suggests agricultural limestone. That is a conditional crop-target rationale, not a lime dose or a universal pH target. Organic matter or cover cropping is also suggested. Actual crop requirements, lime-requirement testing, material analysis, drainage and local suitability must be checked before a rate or fixed treatment; organic matter may improve structure without changing mineral texture class.

reading.title: 5. Keep the four final review models and their evidence separate
paragraphs: The four final-review sets bring together multiple-choice questions, written answers, finished products and practical processes. Set 1 includes a labelled 500 g soil sample and a rapid colour-kit pH test. Set 2 includes five Field B pH readings and a separate Paddock 3 report. Set 3 includes a 5 kg tomato-mix product and texture by the ribbon/feel method. Set 4 includes a crop chart for three soils and a simulated reagent spill. Keep each case's data, methods, instructions and evidence separate. Practising a topic earlier or reading a model answer does not prove completion of its product or process.

The colorimetric rapid-kit task is distinct from Plot C's digital electrode; use the actual kit's chart, instructions and safety procedure for that task. A written response needs review of its reasoning and conditions; filled fields do not prove a correct answer. Each required product or process must be assessed against its own checklist with individual actual evidence. Online reasoning, a model answer and watching a demonstration do not substitute for that evidence.

reading.title: 6. Practise the missing criterion and record what happened
paragraphs: The assessor records 'competent' only when a particular skill has been safely and accurately demonstrated to its defined standard. Otherwise the record says 'not yet demonstrated' and names the gap. For example, correct sample preparation does not make a pH result valid if the meter calibration was wrong. The learner reviews that calibration step, practises it, then performs a new observed attempt.

Record the actual second decision with date, evidence and trainer identity. It may still be 'not yet demonstrated'; offer another targeted practice and attempt as appropriate. Online knowledge attempts are open with directed review, while a practical criterion requires a real observed action. Self-assessment item 5.2 about submitting a report supports reflection; the original self-check table omits cultivator operation/maintenance, so add an honest reflection prompt for those skills without filling a trainer result.

examples.title: Supplied model: Plot C pH 6.8, loam
examples.situation: The source's teaching model reports pH 6.8 and loam, then names tomatoes and corn.
reasoning: Keep pH and texture labelled supplied model rather than personal measurements.
Explain what near-neutral pH and loam texture tend to suggest, and list the unmeasured site/crop constraints.
Treat annual compost and pH monitoring every 1–2 years as examples to check, not compulsory prescriptions.
examples.takeaway: A model supports report writing; it cannot certify all soil conditions.

examples.title: Separate pH 5.8 sandy-loam case
examples.situation: A different case uses pH 5.8, sandy loam, gritty feel and an approximately 0.5-inch ribbon.
reasoning: State the acidity classification source instead of relying on a vague adjective.
Discuss potatoes and strawberries as candidates; corn is conditional on crop/site requirements.

The source's illustrative pH 5.8→6.5 lime-target rationale names corn and alfalfa. Check the actual crop target, an appropriate lime-requirement test and material/site information before turning that example, agricultural limestone or a compost plan into a field recommendation; no dose is established by pH alone.
examples.takeaway: Different source examples and the learner's real Plot C belong in separate report records.

examples.title: A retry can still need more practice
examples.situation: The sample was prepared well, but the pH meter was calibrated incorrectly and its reading is unreliable.
reasoning: The trainer credits observed preparation only under its own criterion and identifies calibration as the unmet one.
The learner studies the actual meter procedure and demonstrates a fresh calibration and measurement.
The trainer records what was actually seen, including another 'not yet demonstrated' if a required check still fails.
examples.takeaway: A new attempt creates new evidence, not automatic success.

glossary: A concise interpretation of available evidence with its limits, not a certificate of complete soil health.
A new assessment after specific feedback and practice, with a new actual decision rather than an automatic pass.
The relevant skill was observed safely and accurately against its stated practical standard.
Required evidence is incomplete or did not meet the criterion; targeted practice and another genuine observation may follow.
The record linking a value to the learner’s sample, date, method, instrument and person who performed the work.
A possible crop based on current evidence, requiring checks of climate, water, drainage and nutrients before a planting decision.

ui.model: Five report sections in a schematic 3D organiser
ui.modelHelp: The five cards illustrate report organisation; stacking them does not create, submit, assess or verify a one-page report. The cards show section order, not measured evidence. No model card represents an actual measurement.
sectionHelp: Use a heading within the one-page report: learner, actual date, Plot C/location and sample identity. Do not invent missing information.
State the grower's purpose and the properties actually investigated, without promising a complete fertility diagnosis.
Link actual pH and texture to sample, method, device/SOP, units and raw observations. Missing results stay pending.
Explain the supported meaning and the unmeasured conditions. Distinguish the two supplied teaching models from your own results.
Name two crop candidates with separate reasons, and at least one supported management next step with limits; no guessed material dose.
